items.title: Photonic Crystal Integrated Graphene-Silicon Schottky Diodes for Resonant Infrared Photodetection
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41701v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Narrowband infrared (IR) photodetection has become a critical technology for the next generation of smart low-power photodetectors. In this work, we present a device based on a graphene-silicon Schottky junction with narrowband response in the short-wave IR (SWIR) regime. Integrating a photonic crystal (PhC) slab in the device enables a wavelength dependant tailoring of graphene absorption. The devices were characterized by photocurrent measurement, which was enhanced more than two orders of magnitude by the PhC integration. The sharp enhancements obtained can also be predicted by numerical simulation. This approach offers a highly scalable, tunable, CMOS-compatible architecture for narrowband IR photodetection, paving the way for next-generation, low-power IR sensors.

items.title: High-efficiency photonic GHZ measurements with linear optics
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41524v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Probabilistic and destructive Bell-measurements, also known as fusions, constitute a fundamental primitive for photonic quantum technologies. These operations rely only on pairwise photonic interference, whereas the computational power of photonic quantum systems originates from many-body interference. Here, we introduce a family of high-efficiency linear-optical GHZ measurements based on four-mode interferometers and show that incorporating many-body interference into this ubiquitous primitive leads to more efficient entangling operations. For the four-photon case, the success probability is $9/32$, and adaptive variants ensure that unsuccessful events project onto useful stabilizer states. We further show that the approach naturally generalizes to larger GHZ measurements, yielding an exponentially higher success probability than previous linear-optical schemes. Finally, we demonstrate practical advantages for graph-state resource generation, entanglement distribution between remote spin-photon interfaces, and fusion-based quantum computing. Our results establish high-efficiency many-body measurements as a new primitive for scalable photonic quantum information processing.

items.title: Metadevices that compute: mathematical foundations and experimental implementations for neuromorphic nanophotonics
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40903v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wave-based analog computing has re-emerged as a compelling alternative to digital electronics for specific linear-algebraic and machine-learning workloads, promising massively parallel, high-bandwidth, and energy-efficient information processing. Metamaterials, metasurfaces, and integrated metastructures (collectively, metadevices) now perform mathematical operations, solve integral and differential equations, multiply matrices, and implement trainable photonic neural networks directly in the wave domain. This focused review consolidates the mathematical foundations that underpin such devices, i.e., the mapping between linear operators and wave scattering, the feedback architectures that realize equation inversion, and the inverse-design and scientific machine-learning toolchains that make their synthesis and training tractable, and connects them to the rapidly growing body of experimental demonstrations, from free-space diffractive processors to reconfigurable guided-wave metastructures. We conclude with open problems and opportunities for this emerging neuromorphic nanophotonics ecosystem.

items.title: Comparison of melanin subtypes using pump-probe microscopy
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40969v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pump-probe microscopy (PPM) is used to probe excited state dynamics of endogenous chromophores to generate contrast that is unavailable in traditional forms of microscopy. Here we apply PPM to characterize melanin, a pigment central to photoprotection, skin and eye pigmentation, and melanoma pathogenesis. Melanin is notoriously difficult to analyze due to its structural and chemical complexity. We imaged melanin from six different lesion categories: cutaneous nevi, lentigo, cutaneous malignant melanoma, conjunctival melanocytic lesions, vulvar melanocytic lesions, and a murine melanoma model, across 21 independent biological samples and 109 regions of interest. Using model fitting, adapted phasor analysis, and support vector machine classification, we characterize and quantify excited-state dynamics as a surrogate for chemical and structural heterogeneity. Heterogeneity of melanin separates cutaneous from non-cutaneous lesions, but is not correlated with malignancy. Benign lentigo is the most heterogeneous population in the dataset, exceeding cutaneous malignant melanoma, while conjunctival lesions are the most homogeneous despite receiving direct solar exposure. Classification on full transient absorption curves separates most subtypes well above the six-class chance level. These findings demonstrate the ability of PPM to reveal subtle differences in melanin photophysics across diverse tissue environments, with implications for optical tissue classification and the understanding of melanoma pathogenesis.

items.title: From proof of concept to practice: the next decade of artificial intelligence in metasurface photonics
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41000v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Over the past decade, artificial intelligence has learned to predict electromagnetic responses rapidly and generate high-performance metasurface designs. However, one question remains open: compared with conventional design workflows that contain no learned model, has it made the complete design workflow faster, and are the resulting devices better? We argue that the answer depends on the task. Reading 100 highly cited optical studies in depth, we distinguish the design tasks in which artificial intelligence is irreplaceable, clearly advantageous, or without clear advantage. In our view, the key to the next decade is not more successes in isolated tasks but making each success a foundation for the field, through shifts such as shared data, trained models, and physics written into learning. Whether artificial intelligence leaves lasting value in this field will depend on whether its benefits can be verified, its methods transferred, and its designs corrected by experiment.

items.title: Optical Quantum Memory Processing for Quantum Hashing
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40904v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sender authentication is an important requirement for secure quantum communication networks. We propose programmable photon-echo quantum memory processing of a multi-time-bin photonic qudit for implementing a quantum-hash-based verification protocol. In this approach, using QM, sender (Alice) generates a quantum hash state by transforming a single stored photonic wave packet into the programmable photonic qudit. Bob's memory coherently maps the received time-bin photonic qudit into a single output mode according to phase encoding. Our scheme relies on a time-resolved coherent detection method introduced here, in which the coherent responses from individual time-bins are sequentially accumulated within Bob's spin coherence prior to the final sender verification. The key advantage of this coherent detection for quantum hashing is shown, and its potential applications are also discussed. The performed analysis demonstrates that experimentally verified parameters of contemporary optical quantum memories enable a proof of principle realization of the proposed architecture. These results reveal an additional role for quantum memories, serving not only as synchronization and repeater resources for long-distance quantum communication, but also as active elements for quantum hashing in conventional quantum key distribution systems.

items.title: Learning Nonlocal Interactions in Large-Scale Heterogeneous Metamaterials through Scientific Machine Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41887v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In multiscale systems, nonlocal interactions among spatially distributed constituents can unlock collective, potentially emergent behavior irreducible to individual constituent responses. Beyond characterization, nonlocality in multiscale systems is increasingly viewed as a design element across fracture mechanics, wave physics, and disordered systems. Existing nonlocality theories provide rigorous descriptions and mechanistic insight, but often require prescribed analytic forms, range, symmetries, or periodicity. Machine learning offers a data-driven route to learn interactions, yet principled approaches that tie the network design to physical theory remain nascent. Here we present domain-decomposition attention neural operator (DANO), which learns configuration-dependent interactions in heterogeneous systems governed by linear field equations from field data alone. Through a case study in large-scale optical metasurfaces, we demonstrate DANO's full-field prediction under geometric heterogeneity and across drive conditions, small-to-large domain transfer, and multifunctional inverse design, with learned interactions validated through physics-based interrogation. As an AI-for-Science tool, it supports interaction discovery and scalable, customizable design of nonlocal multiscale systems, including virtual-reality optics.

items.title: Non-contact temperature sensing and optical scatter in cryogenically-cooled crystalline silicon
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41261v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cryogenic crystalline silicon is a promising optical material for next generation gravitational-wave detectors due to its low mechanical loss (a driver of thermal noise), high thermal conductivity and zero coefficient of thermal expansion at 123 K. In this paper, we report on the design and results of an experiment to measure the temperature of a flat-flat uncoated crystalline silicon sample using a non-contact sensing method relying on interference (optical fringes) made from reflections between the front and back surfaces. We also propose a scheme for implementation of this technique for cryogenic test masses in future gravitational-wave detectors such as Einstein Telescope and LIGO Voyager. Additionally, we characterize the optical scattering of the sample in vacuum at cryogenic temperatures by using a high-sensitivity infrared camera. We measured relatively constant scatter with an average bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) of $(4.43\pm0.2)\times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{sr^{-1}}$ at a scattering angle of $\theta_{s} = 7.5^\circ$ over the (cold-plate) temperature range of 123-294 K and saw no evidence for growth of cryogenic molecular layers (ice) on the sample in our current setup.

items.title: Ultraviolet Raman spectroscopy using multimode aluminum oxide waveguides
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41503v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Waveguide-based Raman spectroscopy offers a route toward compact and integrated photonic sensors. While most waveguide Raman platforms operate in the near-infrared, extending excitation toward the visible and ultraviolet is attractive because shorter excitation wavelengths can provide substantially stronger Raman scattering and access to resonance-enhanced molecular responses. This transition, however, places greater demands on the photonic material because of optical loss, absorption and waveguide-generated spectral background. Here, we investigate aluminum oxide ($Al_2O_3$) waveguides as a low-background platform for Raman spectroscopy at 532 nm and 325 nm using a back-collected excitation and detection geometry. At 532 nm, after normalization to the incident excitation power-time product, the measured $Al_2O_3$ background was more than two orders of magnitude lower than that of $Si_3N_4$. Under 325 nm excitation, the waveguides maintained a weak and reproducible spectral background across the investigated widths. Using immersion oil as a model analyte deposited over the waveguide surface, we demonstrate that analyte-specific Raman fingerprints can be recovered above the waveguide background at both wavelengths. Signal-to-background ratio and spectral contrast were used to quantify analyte visibility relative to the waveguide background, and both metrics consistently confirmed clear detection of the analyte bands. These results demonstrate that $Al_2O_3$ combines low measured spectral background with operation from the visible into the ultraviolet, providing a promising route toward integrated Raman spectroscopy at shorter excitation wavelengths.

items.title: Gearbox cavities: Ultrahigh wave confinement via broken rotational symmetry
items.summary: arXiv:2610.42003v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cavity enhancement of emission from a point source typically relies on structures that preserve its cylindrical symmetry, such as circular Bragg gratings. Combining inverse design with fundamental limits, we show that breaking this symmetry is necessary to maximize the local density of states in lossless two-dimensional cavities. Symmetry-broken designs exceed limits over all cylindrically symmetric structures by up to eight orders of magnitude, acting as ``gearboxes'' that convert the source's emission into high-angular-momentum waves trapped behind a centrifugal barrier.

items.title: Cryogenic Optical Characteristics of S-FPL51 and S-LAH71: Refractive index, Transmission and Thermal expansion
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41481v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Several near-infrared instruments on upcoming extremely large telescopes use a combination of OHARA S-FPL51 and S-LAH71 glass prisms to correct for the atmospheric differential refraction. Because large parts of these instruments are contained within a vessel cooled to liquid nitrogen temperatures, the changes in optical and mechanical properties should be considered during the design phase. In this report, we provide an update to our continuing efforts to characterize the S-FPL51 and S-LAH71 glass under cryogenic conditions. These efforts include a measurement of the refractive index (293 K, 100 K and 80 K), transmission measurements (293 K, 77 K and 43 K) and a determination of the coefficient of thermal expansion (between 293 K and 45 K). We will describe the cryogenic test setups that we have used to obtain our results, and provide summarizing equations of these material properties. This characterization will prove useful for conceptual design trade-offs, mechanical interface solutions and detailed optical design for future near-infrared instrumentation on large telescopes.

items.title: Microscopic Theory of Spin-Orbit Interactions of Light
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40979v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical spin-orbit interactions (SOI), demonstrated experimentally in optical cavities, enable the polarization degrees of freedom of light to be described and controlled as an effective pseudospin, providing a foundation for spintronic-like control of light and the development of next-generation optical technologies. However, prior works describe this emergent effect using phenomenological models that fail to uncover its microscopic quantum origins, and as a result, a rigorous connection between material electronic structure and the optical SOI remains elusive. In this work, we address this fundamental challenge by developing a microscopic quantum theory starting from the non-relativistic quantum electrodynamical (QED) description of light-matter interactions. We show that this effect arises from virtual interactions between confined photons and material excitations. Crucially, our theoretical framework provides microscopic material-design principles for tuning the distinct components of optical SOI, which include the optical birefringence, photonic self-energies, TE-TM splitting, and optical Zeeman splitting, enabling precise engineering of effective magnetic fields, diabolical points, and pseudospin textures. We anticipate that the predictive capability of our microscopic theory will enable systematic screening and design of material systems for photonic spintronics and optical technologies.

items.title: Intensity-Domain Demultiplexing of Orbital Angular Momentum Channels for Optical Communication
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41259v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Orbital angular momentum (OAM) multiplexing has been limited in practice by the complexity and optical loss of the elements that separate the channels at the receiver side. Here we adopt the azimuthal harmonics of OAM petal patterns as the demultiplexing basis, which makes the receiver the optical counterpart of the circular antenna arrays used in radio OAM links: the petal pattern of topological charge $\ell$ carries a single azimuthal harmonic of order $2\ell$, so one Fourier transform of the azimuthal intensity profile returns every channel, without gratings or mode sorters. The petals are formed by projecting a vector vortex beam from a single q-plate onto a linear polarization. A two-channel system at 515 nm with a 16-position circular photoreceiver array reaches 5.2 Gb/s below the forward error correction threshold, 2.6 Gb/s per channel from a 1.4 GHz photoreceiver.

items.title: Dual-rate optical frequency comb based on a cylindrical microresonator with a nanoscale radius variation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41315v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We theoretically find that a cylindrical microresonator with nanoscale radius variation can be a source of coherent microcombs with two repetition rates, independently controlled by the device geometry. This phenomenon arises from the formation of two-dimensional axial-azimuthal dissipative Kerr solitons (2D DKS), which we discovered through numerical simulations of the nonlinearly coupled Lugiato-Lefever equations with realistic microresonator device parameters. We demonstrate that, despite the variation in the dispersion characteristics of azimuthal modes at different axial numbers, the spontaneous synchronization mechanism leads to a unified soliton repetition rate. We consider near-parabolic variations in the radius of a cylindrical resonator, compatible with the surface nanoscale axial photonics (SNAP) platform. In our example, we generate 2D DKS with an azimuthal rate of approximately 329 GHz and an axial rate of 6 GHz, which can be adjusted on demand by selecting the appropriate resonator geometry, thereby promising compact sources of frequency combs operating simultaneously across different frequency scales.

items.title: Non-Hermitian Spectral Topology Shaped by Memory
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41370v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-Hermitian spectral topology has transformed our understanding of bulk--boundary correspondence in open systems, yet its exploration has largely remained within the Markovian regime of instantaneous coupling. Here, we reveal how memory shapes non-Hermitian spectral topology by extending coupling asymmetry from space to time. Spatiotemporal nonreciprocity and memory-induced spectral multivaluedness give rise to nontrivial spectral topology on multi-sheeted Riemann surfaces, governed by both spatial connectivity and interaction history. Coherent interference among long-range memory channels can induce anomalous spectral winding and skin localization opposite to the dominant-coupling direction. Moreover, asymmetric retardation alone can generate non-Hermitian spectral topology and skin accumulation even in the absence of spatial coupling asymmetry. Channel dissipation further drives topological transitions that reverse the skin effect, with a critical point at matched channel and lattice decay rates. We validate the anomalous skin effect and its dissipation-controlled reversal through full-wave simulations and microwave experiments. Our results establish time nonlocality as a fundamental degree of freedom in non-Hermitian topology, revealing phenomena inaccessible within the Markovian paradigm.

items.title: Reconfigurable Generation of Terahertz Spiral Vector Beams Based on All-Dielectric Cascaded Metasurfaces
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41392v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The reconfigurable generation of complex structured terahertz (THz) fields, and vector beams in particular, remains a significant challenge. Here, we propose a novel all-dielectric cascaded-metasurface scheme for the reconfigurable generation of THz spiral vector beams. By combining an isotropic phase-compensation layer with an anisotropic circular-polarization-sensitive layer, together with a new phase design tailored to spiral beams, we achieve independent control of the left- and right-handed circularly polarized (LCP and RCP) components through the relative rotation angle between the two layers. Under linearly polarized THz wave illumination, THz vector beams with switchable spiral numbers of 1-3 and reversible circular-polarization handedness are demonstrated at frequencies around 0.9 THz. Moreover, owing to the longitudinal evolution characteristic of spiral beams, the three generated THz vector beams exhibit azimuthal rotations of 279.9{\deg}, 125.7{\deg} and 75.5{\deg}, respectively, along the propagation direction. Such complex THz vector beams, which combine reconfigurability with longitudinal evolution, are expected to find applications in emerging fields such as next-generation wireless communications and THz imaging. The proposed generation scheme also offers a useful reference for the reconfigurable generation of high-dimensional vector beams.

items.title: The Generalized Twin Image: Understanding Regularized Phase Retrieval
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41531v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Image priors can dramatically improve phase retrieval reconstruction, but their effectiveness strongly varies between imaging modalities. We introduce the generalized twin image, which extends the classical twin-image ambiguity from Fourier phase retrieval to any invertible sensing operator, to understand this effectiveness. The ambiguity extends to undersampled and oversampled measurements, remaining exact under undersampling and for oversampled coded Fourier measurements. We show that it provides a simple criterion to assess regularization effectiveness: the image prior should favor the ground truth over its generalized twin image. We propose the total-variation ratio as a simple measure of this preference, and derive closed-form estimates for structured random phase retrieval models. Experiments with a pretrained denoiser demonstrate that the ratio predicts regularized reconstruction performance across different sensing models.

items.title: Focusing through coupled multimode fibers for miniaturized single-atom tweezer arrays
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-world deployment of quantum technologies requires systems in low SWaP-C packages. Quantum platforms based on ultracold atoms typically trap and control atoms with optical tweezers using light focused through bulky objective lenses, which are costly and sensitive to misalignment. Multimode fibers (MMFs) offer a compact route to focusing light, but their use in forming optical tweezers for cold atoms has been limited to a single fiber. Here we use a 2x1 MMF fused coupler to obtain two independent control paths sharing a common distal facet. We form near-diffraction-limited tweezers through each channel, suppress interference by applying a small frequency offset between the channels, and demonstrate that the tweezer separation is insensitive to misalignment of the input coupling. This work provides a route to reconfigurable single-atom arrays in low SWaP-C environments.

items.title: Field-resolved observation and quantification of the instantaneous Kerr response in semiconductors
items.summary: arXiv:2610.42098v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The optical Kerr effect, whereby the refractive index of a material changes with light intensity, underpins nonlinear photonics and emerging mid-infrared technologies. Accurate determination of the nonlinear refractive index is therefore essential, yet conventional intensity-based techniques infer the nonlinear phase shift indirectly from changes in beam propagation or optical spectra. Moreover, methods such as the $z$-scan cannot resolve the temporal evolution of the nonlinear response, making it difficult to distinguish instantaneous Kerr nonlinearities from delayed contributions, including free-carrier effects. Here, we investigate the nonlinear optical response of germanium at $5 \mu\mathrm{m}$ using field-resolved degenerate pump-probe spectroscopy. By measuring the transmitted probe electric field as a function of pump-probe delay, we directly retrieve the pump-induced phase shift and its temporal evolution while retaining sensitivity to changes in absorption. We observe cross-phase modulation that follows the pump intensity envelope and vanishes when the pump and probe no longer overlap, consistent with an instantaneous Kerr response. The phase shift scales linearly with pump intensity, yielding a nonlinear refractive index of $n_2=(0.87\pm0.16)\times10^{-17} \mathrm{m}^2/\mathrm{W}$. Our results establish the instantaneous Kerr effect as the dominant contribution to the measured nonlinear phase shift under our experimental conditions and demonstrate field-resolved pump-probe spectroscopy as a direct, time-resolved method for determining the nonlinear refractive index and distinguishing instantaneous from delayed optical responses.

items.title: Characteristics of VHF and UHF band detection using Stark shifting in Rydberg-atom sensors
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40952v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a characterization of the sensitivity of broadband electric field measurements in the Very High Frequency (VHF) and Ultra High Frequency (UHF) bands using AC stark shifting of Rydberg states. The dependence of the sensitivity and dynamic range of the field measurements using nD5/2 states of cesium for principal quantum numbers n= 60, 70, 80, 90 and 100 is presented, detailing the intricacies involved. The frequencies considered for the measurement range from 50 MHz to 900 MHz for which a transverse electromagnetic (TEM) cell is used to excite the Rydberg atoms with the RF fields. The corresponding sensitivities achieved are in the $(\mu V/m)/\sqrt{Hz}$ range. A general trend of better sensitivity for higher principal quantum numbers is observed. This work paves the way for a better understanding of the AC Stark dependent field measurements using Rydberg sensors.

items.title: The spin-transfer inverse Faraday effect in Au/YIG thin film bilayers
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41061v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The inverse Faraday effect (IFE) (the generation of an effective magnetic field in a material upon irradiation with circularly polarized light) offers a pathway to ultrafast, non-thermal control of spin dynamics. In metallic/ferromagnetic-insulator (NM/FMI) bilayers, IFE-driven spin polarization in the metallic layer can be an alternative to generate magnon excitations in the magnetic insulator which otherwise would be inaccessible with photon energies below the insulator bandgap, but this avenue has remained mostly unexplored. In this work, we investigate the regime of spin-transfer via IFE in Au/YIG bilayers, by means of ultrafast time-resolved magneto-optical experiments. Understanding the mechanism of this spin-transfer IFE in these NM/FMI heterostructures is crucial for several reasons: it elucidates the fundamental coupling between light's angular momentum and collective spin modes at buried interfaces, it enables all-optical generation and manipulation of pure spin currents, and it paves the way toward THz-frequency spintronic devices leveraging the insulator's long magnon lifetimes.

items.title: Spectral Information Content of Diffraction-Limited Images
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41092v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: High-resolution optical imaging is fundamentally limited by diffraction, which imprints wavelength-dependent structure onto the point spread function (PSF) of the optical system. This intrinsic chromaticity implies that in addition to spatial structure, images encode spectral information. We develop the theory of this spectral information content and provide strategies for its optimal extraction with calculations of Fisher information. We show that polychromatic PSF formation can be expressed as a convolution in logarithmic coordinates and define the corresponding spectral transfer function. We derive this function for the Airy disk and find algebraic decay in spectral log-frequency, implying the existence of arbitrarily fine spectral structure in the ideal, noiseless PSF. We use a differentiable forward model to numerically construct the spectral information eigenbasis and quantify the spectroscopic capability of diffraction-limited imaging across a range of noise and detector systematics. We demonstrate injection and recovery of the constrained spectral modes in a realistic simulated example and compare these results with previously reported methods. Our information-theoretic framework provides a generalisable method for spectral characterisation of PSFs spanning a variety of imaging contexts.

items.summary: arXiv:2610.41198v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this work, we investigate the practical feasibility of achieving a quantum advantage, in the context of inter-satellite quantum communication, of satellite position estimation. The investigation focuses on a quantum-enhanced scheme in which squeezing is added to the derivative mode of a Gaussian probe beam as a means of estimating photon-beam displacement. The performance of the scheme is compared against the standard quantum limit achieved by an optimal classical beam-displacement estimation scheme under a fair same-total-energy constraint. We find that although the benefit provided by squeezing rapidly diminishes as the inter-satellite distance increases due to diffraction-induced beam spreading and subsequent truncation by the finite receiver aperture, a quantum advantage can still be expected over inter-satellite distances up to approximately 100 km under practical satellite configurations. This distance scale between satellites is anticipated for Starlink-type satellite constellations.

items.title: Parametric Enhancement of an Optical Spring in a Dark Signal-Recycling Cavity
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41270v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Optical springs tailor the response of precision sensors. Parametric amplification of the signal field stiffens the spring, extending the precision to higher frequencies. A Michelson interferometer operated at a dark fringe is the most direct way to separate the signal from the carrier for amplification. We experimentally demonstrate such quantum manipulation of the optical spring by placing an optical parametric amplifier in a cavity at the dark port, showing a significant increase of the optical-spring constant with the parametric gain within a factor of four below the oscillation threshold.

items.title: Dipolar Exciton Polarons in a van der Waals Homobilayer
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41730v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Fermi polarons exemplify how many-body interactions give rise to emergent quasiparticles, providing a fundamental framework for understanding interacting quantum matter. In electron-doped two-dimensional semiconductors, exciton polarons offer optical access to Fermi-polaron physics and electrical tunability, yet achieving stronger and more controllable exciton-electron interactions remains a key challenge. Here, we realize dipolar exciton polarons in an electrically tunable van der Waals homobilayer, where interlayer excitons with spatially separated electrons and holes act as quantum impurities carrying permanent electric dipole moments. These dipolar polarons exhibit substantially enhanced exciton-electron interactions, with binding energies more than four times those of conventional intralayer exciton polarons. We further demonstrate that Fermi-sea layer polarization provides an additional degree of freedom for controlling many-body interactions. In particular, the presence of a Fermi sea induces hybridization between oppositely oriented dipolar polarons, whereas confining the Fermi sea to a single layer suppresses this hybridization and produces orientation-selective many-body dressing. Our findings establish an experimental platform for dipolar-polaron physics in which dipole orientation and Fermi-sea layer polarization jointly govern many-body interactions, opening a route towards electrically tunable interactions and dipolar-polaron-mediated attraction between itinerant electrons.

items.title: Standardizing CPO won't matter if the substrate supply chain can’t keep up
items.summary: The success of copackaged optics (CPO) for AI architecture depends on being able to scale the photonics-grade substrate supply chain several times faster than the pluggable-optics supply chain it’s replacing.
items.zh_full: 共封装光学（CPO）在AI架构中的成功，取决于能否将光子级基板供应链的扩展速度，提升到它所替代的可插拔光学供应链的数倍。CPO技术将光学引擎与交换芯片封装在同一基板上，以降低功耗和延迟，但这对基板的制造精度、材料纯度和产能提出了远高于传统可插拔模块的要求。目前，光子级基板的供应链规模远小于可插拔光学供应链，且扩产周期更长、良率控制更复杂。如果基板供应无法跟上CPO的采用速度，即使CPO标准得以统一，其部署也会因关键材料短缺而受阻。行业需要提前规划基板产能投资，并推动供应链上下游协同，否则CPO的规模化应用将面临瓶颈。

items.title: After 40 years of the ‘green problem,’ the quiet laser explains itself
items.summary: Intracavity-doubled green lasers within thousands of laboratories have been quiet for years without anyone knowing why. The answer is the opposite of the obvious one: A nonlinear crystal makes every mode noisier, but the total goes quiet anyway.
items.zh_full: 在数以千计的实验室中，腔内倍频绿激光器多年来一直安静地工作，却无人知晓原因。非线性晶体实际上让每个模式都变得更嘈杂，但总噪声却反而降低了。这一发现解释了长期存在的“绿光问题”——绿激光器在特定条件下表现出异常低的噪声，此前一直缺乏理论解释。研究表明，倍频过程中的非线性相互作用使得各纵模的强度涨落相互关联，导致总强度噪声被抑制。这一机理不仅澄清了四十年的谜题，也为设计低噪声绿光激光器提供了新的理论指导，可能影响光谱学、全息成像等精密应用。

items.title: Quantum dot lasers may unlock next era of AI optical interconnects
items.summary: A misconception about quantum dot lasers (QDLs) is they’re poised to replace indium phosphide (InP) technology. But InP externally modulated lasers (EMLs) will continue serving optical networking and datacom applications, while QDLs emerge for applications that require power efficiency, thermal resilience, and integration density.
items.zh_full: 关于量子点激光器（QDLs）的一个常见误解是它们将取代磷化铟（InP）技术。实际上，InP外调制激光器（EMLs）将继续服务于光网络和数据通信应用，而QDLs则面向需要功率效率、热稳定性和集成密度的新兴应用。量子点激光器因其量子限制效应，在高温下具有更低的阈值电流和更好的温度稳定性，同时支持更高密度的单片集成。这些特性使其特别适合AI光互连场景，其中能效和散热是关键约束。然而，InP EMLs在现有光通信基础设施中仍具有成熟性能和成本优势，短期内不会被完全替代。两种技术将并行发展，各自服务于不同的应用需求。

items.title: How the quantum vacuum perturbs atoms, could shrink black holes and may have helped form galaxies
items.summary: The word "vacuum" may conjure the image of empty space. Maybe you think of a region far outside the solar system without planets, debris, gas clouds or light. According to quantum theory, however, a vacuum is never truly empty. Quantum mechanics extends the Heisenberg uncertainty principle—which states that we cannot measure the position and the velocity of an object exactly at the same time—to a vacuum. The result is that a vacuum can never be still.

items.title: Guarding the Gates of Knowledge
items.summary: A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion. Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must. Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “ I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper ,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses. “He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.” Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. items.title: Scientists reconstruct Van Gogh’s Starry Night sky
items.summary: Vincent van Gogh captured the pre-dawn sky for his iconic painting—in terms of observation and shape when a waning crescent moon, Venus, and the Hyades star cluster appeared close together—so accurately that it led scientists to the exact spot he’d stood 130 years earlier, likely on July 22, 1889.

items.title: Shaping light to see deeper inside biological tissue
items.summary: Integrated wavefront shaping extends the reach of optical imaging to give scientists a deeper and more precise look into biological tissue.

items.title: Meet Oliver Grass, CEO of Assemblify
items.summary: Antonio Castelo, EPIC’s technology manager for bio-medical and lasers, talks to Oliver Grass, CEO of Assemblify, a German developer and manufacturer of custom mechatronic devices, about hyperspectral imaging.

items.title: 780-nm photobiomodulation advances peripheral nerve repair toward a device-ready clinical platform
items.summary: No drug is approved to speed nerve regeneration for peripheral nerve injury, but four decades of research have established 780-nm continuous-wave photobiomodulation (PBM) as a validated, noninvasive treatment for significant motor recovery. We invite industrial partners to bring a translation-ready platform into clinical use.

items.title: Advanced echelle gratings enable high-precision exoplanet detection
items.summary: Spectroscopic measurements of radial velocity are an important tool for exoplanet hunting, and high-resolution gratings are a key enabling technology.
